coach_says: Nc6 is a perfectly sensible developing move against an offbeat opening. If you want to be picky, against a d4 setup the knight in front of the c-pawn means you can't strike with ...c5 easily, so ...c5 or ...Nf6 keep a little more flexibility, but nothing here costs you.
Castling here is fine: your king gets safe and the rook joins the game. Nxc6 first, to break Black's structure before trading on d6, was a touch more accurate, but the difference is tiny.

You had to recapture on c3, and Nxc3 is fine. bxc3 was slightly better because the pawn hits the bishop on b4 with tempo and your knight stays on e2, ready to go to g3 and chase the bishop on f5 before you push f4-f5. When you have a choice of recaptures, ask which one gains time or keeps your pieces on their best route.
1...c6, the Caro-Kann, is a sound main-line reply to 1.e4. Pick the opening you understand; the engine sees no real difference between it and 1...e5, 1...e6 or 1...c5.

Taking on c5 is a reasonable way to open lines, and the position stays balanced. f4, hitting e5 while Black's king is still in the centre, was a little more active, but this is a matter of taste rather than a mistake. Just keep an eye on the strong knight on d4, which eyes c2.
Rae1+ is a strong move: it brings a rook onto the open e-file with check while Black's king is stuck in the centre. Bg6+ and Qxc7 were just as good. You're winning; keep bringing pieces at the king.

Nc3 is natural development and only a little worse than Bg5. Black can answer with ...Bb4 and ...Bg4, harassing your queen on f3, which is the real price of bringing the queen out early. Next time develop the knights and bishops before the queen so she isn't a target.
Kd2 keeps the king in front of Black's queenside pawns and holds the balance, just like Bc2 or d5. The position is equal whatever you choose here, so there is nothing to correct.
h4 is the engine's top choice: with your king tucked on c2 and Black's king on g8, throwing the kingside pawns forward with h4 and g5 to open lines is exactly the right plan. Well played.
also: pawn storm against the castled king

coach_says: Be7 is about as good as anything here. Your position was already difficult because your queen on a8 and king in the centre leave you behind in development, and White is ready to open the centre with exd5. Getting castled quickly is the priority, which Be7 helps with.
c3 to prepare d4 is a reasonable plan. It lets Black hit back in the centre with ...d5 at once, attacking your bishop, so Nc3 or castling first were slightly more natural. The difference is small.
2.Bg5 is a playable system, just a little less flexible than Nf3 or c4. Black's best answer is ...c5 with ideas like ...Qb6 against b2, which your bishop has left behind, so be ready for that.

You have only two pawns for Black's rook, so the game is very hard to save whatever you do. Qd5+ is a fine way to keep checking and look for a perpetual or a trick. Keep the queen active and watch for ...Rh6+ ideas against your king.

When e5 kicked your knight, Ng4 sent it to a square where h3 traps it: every square except h6 loses the knight, and then d5 kicks your other knight and d6 cramps you. Nd5 was the right square, because White has no c- or e-pawn left to chase it away from there, so it sits safely in the centre. When a pawn attacks your knight, look for the square where no pawn can bother it again.

coach_says: Your king is still on d8 with White's rook on d1, and d6 opens the d-file straight at it. After Nb6 your rook has to leave a8, then exd6 leaves a White pawn on d6 next to your king, boxing in your f8 bishop and giving White's rooks the open file. Keep the d-pawn at home while your king sits behind it: b5 followed by ...Bb7 and ...Ra7 develops your queenside pieces without opening lines against yourself.
concept: opening the file to your own king
